tip: 'Gostar' always takes 'de' before what you like, so it is 'gosto de cozinhar' even though English 'like cooking' has no preposition.
'Andar' means floor or storey here: 'o andar de cima' = the floor above. The same word 'andar' also means to walk.
'Ficar' is used to describe how something turned out or ended up. 'Como ficou?' = How did it come out?
'Levar' means to take someone somewhere: 'levar as crianças' = to take the kids. The opposite, 'buscar', means to pick up.
'Marcar' means to book or schedule: 'marcar a consulta' = to make an appointment. Literally it means to mark.
'Pasta' means folder or briefcase, not the food: 'na pasta' = in the folder.
In the past, 'conhecer' means to meet for the first time: 'conheceu' = met. In the present it means to know.
In Brazil 'esse' and 'essa' often mean this, not just that: 'essa carreira' = this career.
'Começar a' + an infinitive means to start doing something: 'começou a trabalhar' (started working).
'Passar' means to spend time: 'passar as férias' = to spend the vacation. Spending money uses 'gastar'.
A they-form verb with no stated subject means they or someone in general: 'não me avisaram' = they didn't tell me.
'No' is the contraction of 'em + o' (in the, masculine). 'Na' is 'em + a' (in the, feminine). Both are mandatory.
'Noite' is feminine: 'a noite'. Time periods: 'a manhã' (morning), 'a tarde' (afternoon), 'a noite' (night). All feminine.
'Precisar de' means to need. The 'de' is required: 'preciso de ajuda', not 'preciso ajuda'. Before an infinitive, many Brazilians drop the 'de'.
Nouns ending in '-ão' are usually masculine: 'o avião', 'o coração', 'o limão'. But some are feminine: 'a mão', 'a televisão', 'a estação'.
'Fazer da vida' is the everyday way to ask about someone's job, so 'O que você faz da vida?' asks what you do for a living.
The 'se' in 'como se diz' makes the verb general (how does one say it), with no specific person. It is the normal way to ask for a word.
'O que você acha de' is the go-to phrase for asking opinions; here 'de' merges with 'essa' to give 'acha dessa ideia'. More common than 'o que você pensa'.
'Fui' is the past form of both 'ir' (to go) and 'ser' (to be). Here 'fui à praia' = I went to the beach; context tells the two apart.
The weekend takes 'no': 'no fim de semana' = on the weekend. 'Fim de semana' is literally end of week.
'Nesse' is the contraction of 'em + esse' (in this). Others: 'neste' = 'em + este', 'naquele' = 'em + aquele', 'nisso' = 'em + isso'.
'Tão + adjective + quanto' means 'as... as': 'tão bom quanto' = as good as. You can also use 'como' instead of 'quanto'.
'Numa' is the contraction of 'em + uma' (in a, feminine). 'Num' = 'em + um' (masculine). Very common in speech.
A definite article makes it specific: 'gosto das músicas' (those songs) vs 'gosto de música' (music in general).
'Mão' is one of the few '-ão' nouns that is feminine: 'a mão'. Its plural is 'as mãos'.
'Sistema' is masculine ('o sistema') despite ending in '-a'. Words of Greek origin ending in '-ma' are usually masculine: 'o tema', 'o cinema', 'o diploma'.
'Vocês' means you all but takes the same verb form as they: 'vocês precisam', 'vocês gostam'.
'Com gás' = sparkling, 'sem gás' = still. You order 'água com gás' or 'água sem gás'.
'Tirar fotos' is the fixed phrase for taking photos; 'tirar' on its own means to pull or remove.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente precisa', never 'a gente precisamos'.
